Summary Erika Maslauskaite, CEO of AlongID, is developing a "missing trust layer" for digital identity, addressing the proliferation of AI fakes and fragmented national ID systems. Her startup aims to unify diverse digital identity providers into a core infrastructure, offering reusable, verified credentials on users' phones, akin to Stripe for payments. This initiative aligns with the EU's eIDAS 2.0 regulation, which mandates digital identity wallets by December 2026, though many member states are behind schedule. AlongID, funded by EU grants and private capital, targets small businesses lacking verification expertise and envisions verifying human accountability behind AI agent transactions. Maslauskaite counters privacy concerns by emphasizing on-device data hashing and the existing digital footprint, arguing that robust digital identity combats widespread fraud. Despite a crowded market, AlongID positions itself as an orchestrator, bridging the gap between rapidly evolving technology and slower regulation. Show More MIAMI, FL - MARCH 04: Christine Rolin passes her iphone over a scanner as she uses the new mobile app for expedited passport and customer screening being unveiled for international travelers arriving at Miami International Airport on March 4, 2015 in Miami, Florida. Miami-Dade Aviation Department and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) unveiled a new mobile app for expedited passport and customs screening. The app for iOS and Android devices allows U.S. citizens and some Canadian citizens to enter and submit their passport and customs declaration information using their smartphone or tablet and to help avoid the long waits in the exit lanes. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images) Getty Images "With AI currently, you can fake everything. You can literally fake everything," Erika Maslauskaite said in an interview. "So then there is a point of trust. So how do we verify what is true and authentic and what is not." Maslauskaite is CEO and co-founder of AlongID, a Lithuanian startup spun out of the software firm Deverium. She calls what she is building "the missing trust layer on the internet." The occasion for building it now is a law. Under the EU's eIDAS 2.0 regulation, in force since May 2024, all 27 member states must offer citizens a digital identity wallet by December 24, 2026. Banks, telecoms and the largest online platforms will be obliged to accept those wallets roughly a year later. The deadline is less than five months away, and it is visibly slipping. Germany has said its state wallet will launch on January 2, 2027, nine days after the legal date. Bulgaria had not started serious work on one as of December, the chairman of Bulgarian eID provider Evrotrust told Biometric Update. The Netherlands has signaled it is likely to miss the deadline, and Malta expects to launch with only partial functionality. The certification schemes the wallets must pass remain unfinished in many capitals, and Lithuania itself only signed a contract in February for a 12-month national wallet sandbox with the Swiss vendor Procivis. European regulation has run ahead of its markets before. "Our digital identity attributes are scattered everywhere. We do not have any control of them," Maslauskaite said. "We are building an ecosystem, connecting all of the different digital identity providers into one core infrastructure." 'It Only Works Now In Poland' Her favorite exhibit is Poland. The government super-app mObywatel has 12 million users, a base that doubled in 30 months. "But it only works now in Poland," Maslauskaite said. Europe already has plenty of national wallets, in her telling, but "those are local solutions." MORE FOR YOU Ukraine's Diia app is her other example. "The moment people fled the country, you know it was gone," she said. "You would need to carry your passport." The Polish spinoff Diia.pl counts as a residence permit for refugees, not a passport. India's DigiLocker, a document wallet built on top of the Aadhaar identity system, launched in 2015 and now holds credentials for more than 530 million registered users. Singapore's Singpass covers roughly 97% of citizens and permanent residents over 15. None of these systems talk to each other. Businesses pay for that fragmentation on every onboarding. "The camera opens with scan your face. Then you would scan your passport," she said of the standard bank signup, a check the customer repeats at the next bank, and the next country, while the firm pays a vendor each time. "There is no point for them paying for the repetitive process," Maslauskaite said. Her model puts a verified, reusable credential on the user's phone and charges for the orchestration behind it. "The wallet is just the output," she said. "The core thing is trust infrastructure." The template is payments. "There are plenty of the local payment methods that Stripe connected into one core infrastructure," she said. Identity providers plugged into her network get paid when a credential is reused: "We are changing the business model, same as Spotify did for music." 'The Project Of Three Years' The idea is seven years old, Maslauskaite said, and it started inside a bank. Her brother was working at GBG, the London-listed identity verification group, she said, and watched what it took to plug a verification vendor into a bank with branches in ten countries. "It's like the project of three years," she said. Rules change mid-build, technical requirements change, the business changes. GBG, headquartered in Chester, later became a Deverium partner, and today it sits alongside Regula, iProov and Aware on AlongID's list of connected providers. The build is funded by a €1.97 million grant co-financed by the EU and Lithuania's economy ministry, running from January 2024 through July 2026, plus roughly €1 million of the company's own capital, by her account. AlongID debuted at Mobile World Congress in Barcelona in March 2025 and is not yet commercially live. Publicly disclosed pilots include a European neobank, a central bank and Lithuania's Centre of Registers. The first launch, she says, is weeks away: business account opening with an Estonian neobank she did not name. The customers she describes are not the giants with compliance departments. Small firms "lack expertise in terms of identity verification and regulation and compliance," she said, and "they're not capable of securing digital identity solutions currently." Her example is a ten-person accounting firm that is legally exposed if it fails to verify a client company, its shareholders and its CEO. 'No One Is Trying To Establish The Big Brother' Asked in the interview whether a bloc-wide identity layer amounts to a permanent government file on everyone, Maslauskaite pushed back. "No one is trying to establish the big brother here," she said. Nothing pools in a central database, she argues. "Everything is on the device and everything is hashed," she said. "We just know the hash." Her blunter point is that the tracking already exists. "You have your passport, you have your social media accounts, you have your Google account, you have your bank account," she said. Between regulators and platforms, "you're being like checked everywhere." The privacy fight over eIDAS 2.0 was real. While the law was being drafted, Mozilla and Cloudflare fought a provision requiring browsers to trust government-designated website certificate issuers. An open letter from more than 500 security researchers across 39 countries called it machinery a repressive government could abuse. Lawmakers backed down on part of it. The final text dropped an earlier plan for a single persistent identifier attached to every wallet holder. It added a right to use pseudonyms, and services cannot penalize people who decline the wallet. The Vienna-based digital rights group epicenter.works has argued those paper safeguards are not fully mirrored in the technical framework member states are actually building. "I always think of privacy and anonymity as completely different things," Varun Kabra, chief growth officer at Concordium, said on the On The Margin podcast. His layer-1 blockchain puts a verified-human check behind every account and hides the identity with zero-knowledge proofs. The public is not sold. In the UK, a petition against the government's proposed digital ID scheme drew nearly 3 million signatures, among the largest in the country's history. When age verification under the Online Safety Act switched on in July 2025, Proton VPN reported signups jumping more than 1,400% within minutes. Maslauskaite answers with fraud: "how much fraudulent activities are currently happening, how much stolen identities do we have," she said. Stolen credentials feed a crime economy estimated at $51 billion in crypto alone. The risk runs the other way too: in banking, automated risk signals already cut customers off with no human in the loop. 'Behind Every Agent' The forward-looking half of her pitch is not about people at all. "Behind every agent you would need to verify who's acting," Maslauskaite said. If an AI agent renews her phone contract, she wants the telco to know it acted "on my behalf, not on someone else." She points to Sintra, a Vilnius-born startup selling AI helper avatars to small businesses, which raised a $17 million seed round in June 2025. American small firms adopt those agents fastest, she argues, because the market is lightly regulated; in Europe there is no accepted way to prove who stands behind one. The institutions on the other side agree the gap exists, which is why most banks block AI agents from touching customer money at all. Kabra sees the same hole. When an AI agent books a flight, "the counterparty on the other side, the airline in this case, or the ticketing platform, whatever it is, they have no way to verify where a real accountable human is behind the transaction," he said. "Our entire financial ecosystem was primarily human-centric," Chandler Fang, founder of t54 Labs, said on the On The Margin podcast. His company builds verification infrastructure between AI agents and payment rails . Depositing investor money at a branch, he said, he asked himself "why I never feel anxious or nervous or concerned when I'm deciding to put two million dollars into Chase bank account." Moving the same money into a crypto wallet, "I need to double check, I need to triple check." Maslauskaite has even floated taxing verified agents as automation eats payroll receipts, so that software workers help fund the social security systems human workers are leaving. 'A Very High Entry Market' The identity verification industry she is entering generates somewhere in the mid-teens of billions of dollars a year, with 2026 estimates ranging from about $14 billion to $18 billion, and it is crowded: Sumsub, Jumio, Didit and dozens of other vendors sell checks, while wallet-native players like Procivis and Signicat chase the same eIDAS rails. "It's a very high entry market to be in," Maslauskaite conceded. Her rebuttal to the obvious question, why a startup from a country of 2.8 million ends up as the connective tissue, is to reject the framing. "Our vision is not to become a monopoly," she said. "We're just the mediator, the orchestrator, but not the aggregator." The gap between the mandate and the rollout does not appear to worry her. "The technology develops way more quicker than the regulation," she said. Editorial Standards Reprints & Permissions LOADING VIDEO PLAYER... FORBES’ FEATURED Video

Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Reuters View image in fullscreen The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has announced an independent review of the protective security provided by the state. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Reuters UK security and counter-terrorism Mahmood orders urgent security review after killing of Ann Widdecombe Home secretary also expands police support ‘with immediate effect’ for high-profile public figures not currently MPs Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Mon 12 Oct 2026 14.20 EDT Last modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 14.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Security arrangements for high-profile public figures including politicians and members of the royal family are to be urgently reviewed after the killing of Ann Widdecombe , the home secretary has said. Shabana Mahmood said former MPs, party leaders who are not MPs, peers, former members of devolved parliaments and party spokespeople will also be offered police support. The UK’s protective security system will be re-examined to combat the growing risks of terrorism, extremism and state threats, as well as harassment and intimidation, Mahmood said. The review will be carried out by Sir Stephen Lovegrove, a former UK national security adviser, who will look at whether current security arrangements ensure there is adequate protection for those most at risk. This includes high-profile individuals such as members of the royal family, government ministers, MPs, locally elected representatives and other prominent individuals in British politics. His review will not include an assessment of individual cases. Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokesperson, was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon , having sustained serious injuries. Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with Widdecombe’s murder. He is also accused of “online reconnaissance” of prominent people and institutions, travelling to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage’s home in south London on 19 April 2025 and trying to break into it 15 months before Widdecombe was killed. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards ‘almost certainly’ behind RAF Fairford threats, says Burnham Read more Addressing the Commons, Mahmood said that, regardless of the outcome of the investigation into an attempted break-in at Farage’s home, it is “clear there is insufficient protection for those who serve”. “I can therefore announce today that I will expand, with immediate effect, police support to political figures who are not currently members of parliament,” she said. “This will include former members of parliament, peers and party spokespeople, giving them access to a named police officer, as well as help with wider security measures. Mahmood added: “Today I also announce an independent root-and-branch review of the protective security provided by the state to those in public life. We can defeat those who mean us harm, but we are strongest when we act together. “In a more dangerous world, we are faced by threats from without and within that target our democracy and our way of life. In response, we are adapting and strengthening our defences. “As ever, I commend the work of the police and our security services, who labour in silence to keep us safe. And I’m sure the whole house joins me in offering thanks to them for that vital life-saving work.” Lovegrove will look at how existing security is provided, whether funding and other measures are being used effectively and proportionately, and how decision-making can be more consistent in response to threat and risk. Robert Buckland is conducting a separate review into the murder of Sir David Amess MP , which will consider the security of MPs in their constituencies. In May’s local elections the Electoral Commission found that 55% of all candidates experienced some form of harassment and intimidation, as did the same proportion of candidates at the 2024 general election. Photograph: Pier Marco Tacca/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels. Photograph: Pier Marco Tacca/Getty Images Ukraine Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House Europe live – latest updates Jennifer Rankin in Brussels and Andrew Roth in Kyiv Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.39 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House. Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia. The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump . Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’ Read more Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after an purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold. “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.” Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes , although the Ukraine war was also significant. Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network , to prevent it from being used on drones flying above 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed. View image in fullscreen Firefighters working at the scene of a Russian drone strike in a residential area in Kyiv on Thursday. Photograph: Vincenzo Circosta/Anadolu/Getty Images Speaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal. “Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.” Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed. Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones. Starlink is produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, but controlled by the US government . When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump. View image in fullscreen Zelenskyy with the presidents of the European Council, Antonio Costa (left) and the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen (right) on Friday. Photograph: Pier Marco Tacca/Getty Images According to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70 bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.” The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments from a €90bn funding plan agreed last December that was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan. The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan. Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative. “We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said. The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states. Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire, “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions and adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy Donald Trump SpaceX European Union Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.bursa.ro/great-wall-motor-en.text: Great Wall Motor (GWM) will produce the Ora 5 compact SUV in Bulgaria, starting in 2027, under a manufacturing agreement with a local partner. This will mark the Chinese automaker's first production base in Europe, Reuters reports. Great Wall Motor announced yesterday that the Bulgarian plant will have a planned capacity of 50,000 vehicles per year, with production set to begin in the first quarter of next year. Financial details of the agreement have not been disclosed. Chinese automakers are rushing to establish production bases in Europe to support sales growth and reduce exposure to trade barriers, following the European Union's imposition of additional tariffs on electric vehicles manufactured in China, alongside discussions with Beijing regarding limits on hybrid vehicle imports. Currently, GWM electric vehicles imported from China are subject to the standard 10% tariff applied to automobile imports into the European Union, plus an additional 20.7% anti-subsidy duty. "We don't just want to sell cars in Europe; we want to become part of Europe," stated GWM Chief Technology Officer Nicole Wu. Last year, a GWM executive stated that the Chinese manufacturer aims to produce 300,000 vehicles in Europe by 2029. "Looking ahead, the group plans to develop integrated industrial parks in Europe, dedicated to vehicles and components," the company stated in a recent press release. GWM currently sells the Ora 5 model in Europe with electric, hybrid, and gasoline powertrains. The company did not specify which of these versions would be manufactured at the plant in Bulgaria. * GWM's plans for Europe: new models and an expanded offering beyond electric vehicles GWM's plans for Europe include the launch of at least ten new models-or variants thereof-over the next two years, as well as the expansion of its product lineup beyond electric vehicles. Since 2021, GWM has operated a research and development center in Munich, Germany, which focuses on analyzing local demand, ensuring regulatory compliance, and validating products. As one of the first Chinese automakers to enter the European market, GWM launched a major, electric-vehicle-focused offensive earlier this decade; however, it has struggled to gain a foothold. While Chinese rivals such as BYD, Chery, and Leapmotor have seen rapid growth in the region, GWM's sales have remained negligible-dropping by nearly 30% in 2025 to just 3,500 vehicles. Great Wall Motor has set a goal to reach a market share of 3%-5% in Europe by 2030. * Geely scouting locations for a European plant Chinese automaker Geely is evaluating several locations for a plant in Europe but has yet to reach a final decision regarding local production, according to sources cited by Reuters, as reported by Agerpres. When asked whether the Chinese manufacturer would build a plant in the region, Li Chuanhai-vice president of Geely Auto Group, one of the brands under the Zhejiang Geely Holding Group-stated last month: "We haven't reached the 100% mark yet." Discussions are ongoing between Geely and the new Polish government regarding the joint construction of a plant to produce electric vehicles in Poland; however, several officials previously told Reuters that they do not view Geely as an ideal partner. "We have several options," Li Chuanhai said when asked about the progress of the talks, without providing further details. Meanwhile, Nicolas Appelgren, head of European operations for the Lynk & Co brand, confirmed that Geely is considering multiple locations in the region. Lynk & Co-a brand within the Geely portfolio that currently sells only a hybrid model in Europe-launched a battery-electric vehicle in Italy this month and plans to manufacture its next battery-electric model in Europe. Geely is the second-largest Chinese automaker, trailing only BYD. The Geely Group controls Volvo Cars, operates a joint venture with Renault, and holds stakes in Aston Martin and Mercedes-Benz. * China Becomes Global Leader in Vehicle Sales In 2025, Chinese automakers surpassed their Japanese counterparts in global vehicle sales for the first time, marking a major shift in the global automotive industry, according to a report by *Nikkei* cited by Xinhua in March. Total global sales by Japanese automakers fell to approximately 25 million units last year, causing the country to lose its leading position for the first time since 2000. Meanwhile, Chinese automakers sold nearly 27 million units worldwide in 2025, securing the top spot globally. According to the report, BYD overtook Ford (USA) to reach sixth place globally, while Geely surpassed Honda (Japan) to secure eighth place. Six Chinese automakers-including Chery, Changan Automobile, SAIC Motor, and Great Wall Motors-entered the global top 20, outnumbering the five Japanese manufacturers on the list. In the electric vehicle (EV) segment, BYD surpassed Tesla, becoming the world's leading seller of electric vehicles last year. Tang Jin, an automotive sector expert and analyst at the Japanese group Mizuho Bank, explained that China's rise to the top position represents more than just a change in rankings; it signals a restructuring of the global automotive industry, driven by China's successes in technology, profitability, and rapid progress in research and development. In his view, Japan must re-evaluate its strategies regarding electrification and its positioning in the global market, in response to growing competition. Articol despre automotive, China, Bulgaria.
